# How did the original poster ultimately make TSID work in simulation and real machine, and what parts can only be considered as specific robot hacks?

> **Current answer:** The author ultimately did not use real floating base states. He reported two important hacks for the real machine: first, recompute forward kinematics using measured joint states and adjust the TSID reference based on end-effector pose error; second, add small biases to the hip and ankle joints after QP computation to reduce large tracking errors during weight shift. The author explicitly stated that the simulation and real machine can run, but no bias values, integral bounds, stability metrics, or other robot reproducibility data were provided, so these can only be considered as specific engineering records and cannot be replicated.

## Key terms

- Forward kinematics (FK) (正向运动学)
- End effector (末端执行器)
- Joint offset (关节偏置)
- Weight shift (重量转移)

## Problem and symptoms

- Can a position control robot directly use real joint/float base states to compute TSID QP and then integrate virtual state to find position commands?
- What can the real machine do if real states are not directly fed into TSID?
- System runs when only integrating virtual or command state; system diverges after real state QP and task error calculation.
- Real floating base ground truth or estimator state directly feeds back and still causes instability.
- Large tracking errors occur in hip and ankle joints during weight shift.

## Environment

- TSID; Gazebo with PyBullet; position control robot; practitioner cited iCub/Talos, questioner validated in an unspecified real machine.

## Priority diagnostics

- Distinguish QP used state, integral start, and base position PID feedback; check if a_sol corresponds to q_real but uses q_tsid integral.
- Confirm joint feedback is closed via base position servo; separate floating base/contact stability from joint position closed-loop.

## Possible causes

- Real state enters both TSID and base position controller, causing double feedback.
- Acceleration derived from real state is from another virtual state integral, which is inconsistent.

## Attempts

- Maintainer provided virtual state TSID and force/torque control boundaries; practitioner shared model state TSID with foot F/T/IMU stabilizer; questioner attempted real floating base, Cartesian end-effector error integration, contact reference, and gain adjustment.

## Effective fixes

- Generic and clean internal thread is to use joint torque control; position control robots typically run TSID with virtual state and modify CoM reference via F/T or IMU stabilizer.
- The questioner's specific real machine solution is to not use real floating base state, recompute end-effector pose from measured joints, and add small biases after QP.

## Result

- The questioner reported the solution works in simulation and real machine; thread does not provide stability margin, parameter range, or cross-robot replication.

## Limitations

- Maintainer explicitly stated he does not know the clean, general solution of directly feeding real states into position control TSID.
- End-effector error integration and joint bias are claimed hacks by the questioner and cannot be directly considered as general parameters for other robots.
- Discussion on contact reference height, landing rebound, and swing/contact gain has not formed a maintained, unified rule.

## Safety notes

- Before applying biases and integral references in real machine, set amplitude, speed, and integral saturation boundaries and gradually verify in protected conditions; original post does not provide these safety boundaries.
